doc.title: Jerry Bergonzi interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 7, 2022

title: Jazz and society across decades; jazz peaked in 1965
summary: Asked about social connections of jazz through the decades, he jokes that the jazz universe peaked in 1965 and contrasts it with today's access to transcriptions and recordings.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Um hum. Very interesting. The other day I heard John Coltrane’s “A Love Supreme” part of it. They played part of it on Sirius radio. And I started thinking about the certain decades of jazz. And it seems like for much of jazz there was a social connection that went with the music and I’m not sure I’m correct about this but in the 30s you had a dance and entertainment element. In the 50s — when I think of the 50s I think of you know there’s this sort of hipster — Dizzy Gillespie with the beret, like there’s a hip- jiveness to it. And then in the 60s you had a Civil Rights element and a lot of spirituality. And I think about the current times now and I don’t know what is the — is there a social aspect connected to jazz that is recognizable?

Yeah. People often ask me where is jazz going. And I said you need to ask young people because they have their finger on the pulse of the music. They know everything is coming out, they know that. So I don’t know if I’m even qualified to answer that. And I agree with you about the 60s. In a joking way I say yeah the jazz universe peaked in ’65 you know. When everybody was alive and well. You know, Ben Webster was alive and well. Coleman Hawkins was alive and well. Sonny Rollins doing his thing. John Coltrane raging. The Miles Davis Quintet. You know everybody is alive and well. The avante garde alive and well. The swing guys, the bebop guys, the hard hop guys. You know? Alive and well and playing this great music. And being a student of it, I didn’t differentiate well this is hip, that’s not that hip, this is — you know. But today everything is in retrospect. You know these people in those schools aren’t — they’re not alive, a lot of these players. So it’s a different, and not to mention the iPhone and the computers. You know you want to sound like Clifford Brown? There’s probably every song he’s ever played already transcribed. Here’s his favorite licks, his favorite — this is what he practiced. The same thing with John Coltrane of course, Joe Henderson and Sonny Rollins. It’s there on a silver platter. And you want this recording? Yes, easy to get. You can have every record on a little thumb drive. You know? Whereas back in my day you couldn’t get all the recordings you know. And somebody said to me, “Yeah and back in my generation we listened to one recording a thousand times. Today you listen to a thousand recordings once.” You know? I get it. It’s different. Whether somebody’s

playing music for social reasons I wonder. But I can say this though the world has gone so materialistic. How many things can they have? Let’s get some more things. Things, things, things. But for musicians, just to play music, that’s pretty amazing.
